The request

Subject: Evidence needed for the checkout launch decision
PH
VP of Product and Head of Operations
To: Product Analytics Specialist (you)

Hi Product Analytics team,

We need to decide whether the new checkout is ready for a wider launch. Please separate evidence that a change exists from evidence that it is worth making. Use eligible users as the denominator, check customer complaints, and show the dollar impact.

Specifically, I need answers to 4 questions:

  1. 1. Did recorded satisfaction clear our goal?
    Compare the survey mean with the stated satisfaction goal. Tell me what the test can say about the recorded respondents, and whether those respondents can stand for all our users.
    Part A
  2. 2. Did checkout B improve purchase conversion?
    Use the randomized A and B groups to test the difference. Show the size of the observed lift and a 95% interval. Keep the test result separate from any business hurdle.
    Part B
  3. 3. Does the purchase evidence justify a launch after complaints and costs?
    Compare complaint rates with our stated limit. Then account for extra purchase margin, rollout cost, and excess complaint cost. Give me a provisional decision supported by all three checks.
    Part C
  4. 4. Does your decision still hold after an evidence audit?
    Recheck the workbook against the supplied formula explanations and the H1, H2, and H3 software output. Keep your own decision, but revise its explanation if a denominator, test comparison, or limitation was missing.
    Take-home

For your own review:

  • Keep your workbook and checkpoint copies locally for your own review. This is ungraded practice; nothing is submitted.

Please make it easy to trace each claim back to a cell or an output table.

Best,
VP of Product and Head of Operations
CedarCart

📎 cedarcart_ab_test.csv📎 S06P_Learning_Workbook.xlsx

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part A · answers email question 1

Part A · Is recorded satisfaction different from CedarCart’s goal?

⏱ 10 min
From slide 27 → work this card → Back to slide 28 · bring: Calculated t-statistic of 1.00 and p-value of 0.333 confirming failure to reject the 70-point benchmark.

What the session covered · Section 1 Hypothesis Testing Logic, Errors, and Benchmark Mean Comparisons

Start at IN-CLASS_Lab Part A!B7. Read the supplied sample size, mean, sample spread, goal, and degrees of freedom. This is a one-sample t-test: it compares one group’s average score with a fixed goal. It does not compare checkout A with checkout B.

  • The question: The null claim H0H_0 says the population mean equals the goal; the two-sided alternative H1H_1 says it differs.
  • The calculation: The standard error SE=s/nSE=s/\sqrt n measures uncertainty in the sample mean; t=(xˉ−μ0)/SEt=(\bar x-\mu_0)/SE measures its distance from the goal in standard-error units.
  • The decision: Compare the two-sided p-value with the chosen cutoff α\alpha; a large p-value does not prove H0H_0 true.

A Type I error rejects a true null claim. A Type II error misses a real difference. Neither error is fixed by calling a small survey representative. After calculating B9:B11, inspect H1 before choosing B13. At home, explain your choice in B14 and caption the H1 evidence in B17. Say clearly whether the recorded respondents can speak for all 800 users.

SE=sn=C7B7=B9 SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}=\frac{\text{C7}}{\sqrt{\text{B7}}}=\text{B9} t=xˉ−μ0SE=B8−D7B9=B10 t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{SE}=\frac{\text{B8}-\text{D7}}{\text{B9}}=\text{B10} df=n−1=B12,pt=2P(Tdf≥∣t∣)=B11 df=n-1=\text{B12},\qquad p_t=2P(T_{df}\geq |t|)=\text{B11}

Before the timer · instructor demo

Follow along: in SPSS, run the H1 block and leave H1 Satisfaction Benchmark open.

SPSS block for this part · already in your syntax file

You do not type this: it is already in S06P_SPSS.sps, the one syntax file you use all session. Once per SPSS session, run the CD line and the H0 block first (the setup code is above). * Lecture connection: One-Sample t-Test for Benchmark Goals .
* Why: Test recorded satisfaction against the fixed source-checked 70-point goal .
* How: TESTVAL sets the fixed goal; VARIABLES selects satisfaction and excludes blank scores .
* How: CI(.95) requests the 95% interval for the difference from the goal .
* Read the result: Read H1 N, mean, sample SD, t, df, two-sided significance and whether the difference interval covers zero .
* Watch out: Do not interpret the difference-from-goal interval as a between-arm interval .
* Run: After H0, find H1 in the supplied Syntax Editor and select the complete block .
* Run: Choose Run > Selection, not Run > All for this single block .
* Run: Switch with Window to Output Viewer and find H1 One-Sample Statistics and Test .
TITLE 'H1 Satisfaction Benchmark'.

TEMPORARY.
* Keep only the rows that meet the condition (others are deleted).
SELECT IF (malformed_any=0).

T-TEST /TESTVAL=70 /MISSING=ANALYSIS
 /VARIABLES=satisfaction /CRITERIA=CI(.95).

✅ Done when: Cell B11 displays a p-value of 0.333. Save.
⚠️ Most common mistake: Treating a test that does not reject the goal as proof that every CedarCart user meets the goal. The test concerns a mean, and the recorded respondents may not represent all users.
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • B9 looks too large. Divide C7 by SQRT(B7), not by B7.
  • B10 has an unexpected sign. Subtract the goal in D7 from the sample mean in B8.
  • B11 is one-sided. Use T.DIST.2T(ABS(B10),B12); B12 supplies the degrees of freedom.
Why does the survey’s reach matter?

The t-test describes uncertainty from having a limited number of recorded scores. It cannot repair a survey process that favored some users over others. In B14, keep the test conclusion and the question of representation in separate clauses.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part B · answers email question 2

Part B · How strong is the evidence that checkout B changes purchase conversion?

⏱ 10 min
From slide 51 → work this card → Back to slide 52 · bring: Calculated z-statistic of 2.843 and 95% CI [3.14, 16.86] percentage points for checkout conversion.

What the session covered · Section 2 A/B Testing with Proportions and Statistical Uplift

Start at IN-CLASS_Lab Part B!B7. Each arm’s denominator is its eligible randomized users, not its active sessions. A two-proportion z-test asks whether the observed purchase-rate gap could arise when the true arm rates are equal. Under that null claim, it uses one pooled purchase rate.

  • Test: Use the pooled rate p^0=(xA+xB)/(nA+nB)\hat p_0=(x_A+x_B)/(n_A+n_B) to calculate the null standard error SE0SE_0, then divide the observed difference Δ\Delta by SE0SE_0.
  • Effect interval: Use the supplied unpooled error SEΔSE_\Delta around Δ\Delta for the 95% interval; it answers how large the true gap might be.
  • Units: A difference between two rates is reported in percentage points, not as a relative percent change.

A small p-value supports a difference; it does not show that the entire interval clears CedarCart’s business hurdle. Check the two claims separately. Enter B9:B12 and B14:B15, then inspect H2 and choose B18 without copying an answer from this guide. At home, explain the test and hurdle comparison in B19. In B22, name the H2 tables and compare its uncorrected Pearson result with the workbook test.

The equations you are building

p^0=xA+xBnA+nB=C7+D7B7+B8=B9,SE0=p^0(1−p^0)(1nA+1nB)=B10 \hat p_0=\frac{x_A+x_B}{n_A+n_B}=\frac{\text{C7}+\text{D7}}{\text{B7}+\text{B8}}=\text{B9},\qquad SE_0=\sqrt{\hat p_0(1-\hat p_0)\left(\frac1{n_A}+\frac1{n_B}\right)}=\text{B10} Δ=pB−pA=B16,z=ΔSE0=F7−E7B10=B11,pz=2(1−Φ(∣z∣))=B12 \Delta=p_B-p_A=\text{B16},\qquad z=\frac{\Delta}{SE_0}=\frac{\text{F7}-\text{E7}}{\text{B10}}=\text{B11},\qquad p_z=2\bigl(1-\Phi(|z|)\bigr)=\text{B12} L=Δ−1.96SEΔ=B14,U=Δ+1.96SEΔ=B15,SEΔ=B13 L=\Delta-1.96SE_\Delta=\text{B14},\qquad U=\Delta+1.96SE_\Delta=\text{B15},\qquad SE_\Delta=\text{B13}

⚠️ Most common mistake: Using the pooled standard error for the effect interval. B10 is for testing equal rates; the interval uses the supplied unpooled standard error in B13.
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • The pooled rate exceeds 100%. Divide total purchases by total eligible users in B9; do not multiply the formula by 100.
  • The z sign seems reversed. B11 uses the B rate in F7 minus the A rate in E7.
  • H2 does not match B11. Compare B11 squared with H2’s uncorrected Pearson chi-square, not its continuity-corrected row.
Why are the two standard errors different?

The test temporarily assumes equal true purchase rates, so it combines the purchases to estimate one rate. The effect interval does not make that equality assumption. It estimates uncertainty using each arm’s observed rate. That is why B10 and B13 have different jobs.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part C · answers email question 3

Part C · Do complaints and costs change the checkout launch case?

⏱ 10 min
From slide 74 → work this card → Back to slide 78 · bring: Calculated net loss of -$360 and verified guardrail breach leading to recommendation against rollout.

What the session covered · Section 3 Practical Significance, Guardrail Metrics, and Cross-Tool Reconciliation

Start at IN-CLASS_Lab Part C!B7. A guardrail is a limit on harm that matters alongside the main purchase measure. First calculate complaints per eligible user in each arm. Then compare the B-minus-A complaint gap with the supplied limit in B12. Finally calculate the experiment’s net dollar impact.

  • Complaint rates: Each arm’s complaint count is divided by that arm’s eligible users; the gap Δc\Delta_c is in percentage points.
  • Net impact: Value extra purchases at margin, then subtract B rollout cost and the cost of excess complaints.
  • Reconcile: For a two-by-two table, the uncorrected Pearson result χ2\chi^2 matches the squared corresponding proportion statistic z2z^2.

Do not let one purchase p-value make the whole launch decision. The business rule needs purchase evidence, the complaint limit, and economics together. Enter B9:B11 and B13. Inspect H3, then write your own provisional sentence in B15 and save the Completed snapshot. At home, add the H3 caption in B19. Expand B15 to cover the decision, both outcomes and net impact, and one limit on what this experiment establishes.

⚠️ Most common mistake: Making the launch choice from the purchase p-value alone. A statistically detectable purchase difference does not waive the complaint limit or pay the rollout and complaint costs.
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • Complaint rates look too high. B9 uses C7/B7 and B10 uses D7/B8; format the fractions as percentages without multiplying by 100.
  • The complaint gap has the wrong direction. B11 is B10-B9, so it is B minus A.
  • Net impact omits a cost. In B13, include B rollout cost for every B user and excess complaint cost, as well as extra purchase margin.
Why check complaints even when purchases improve?

A checkout can make purchase easier while also creating service problems. A guardrail makes that trade-off visible before a wider launch. H3 tests whether complaint rates differ; B11 and B12 address the size of the gap against CedarCart’s limit. Neither check replaces the dollar calculation in B13.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part C · answers email question 4

Take-home · Does your CedarCart decision survive a careful recheck?

⏱ 15 min
At home → work this card → Save locally

What the session covered · Section 3 Practical Significance, Guardrail Metrics, and Cross-Tool Reconciliation

Start at IN-CLASS_Lab Part C!B15, where you left your provisional decision. This revisit is an audit, not a new experiment. Check the calculations and the words used to explain them. A p-value addresses a test claim. An interval addresses plausible effect sizes. A guardrail and net impact address the business decision.

  • Part A: Compare B10:B11 with H1, then check that B14 does not turn evidence from recorded respondents into a claim about every user.
  • Part B: Compare the workbook test with H2’s uncorrected Pearson row; check the eligible-user denominators and explain the interval-to-hurdle comparison in B19.
  • Part C: Compare B9:B11 and B13 with the supplied inputs, caption H3 in B19, and revise B15 in your own words.

The classic error is to treat a software label, a small p-value, or an early choice as the whole answer. Use the visible diagnostic checks to catch formula problems. Then write three short sentences in B15: your decision, the purchase and complaint evidence with net impact, and a limitation. Do not change a sound decision merely because you are revisiting it. Do change an explanation that does not match its evidence.

Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • H2 and Excel appear to disagree. Square Part B B11 and use H2’s uncorrected Pearson row for the comparison.
  • Your memo calls a rate gap a percent change. Describe Part B’s effect bounds and Part C B11 in percentage points.
  • B15 has only a verdict. Add the purchase evidence, the B11-to-B12 complaint check, B13 in dollars, and one limitation.
What does cross-tool agreement establish?

Agreement between the workbook and software is a useful check on arithmetic, denominators, and the selected test row. It does not prove that a survey represents all users or that an experiment will have the same effects after a wider rollout.

Topic 1 · Reproduce the in-class parts Reproduce

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

ExcelTrace Parts A, B, and C in the workbook Parts A, B, C

Reopen IN-CLASS_Lab Part A, IN-CLASS_Lab Part B, and IN-CLASS_Lab Part C. Check the formula cells and visible diagnostics. Trace the inputs for Part C B13 without changing your submitted workbook.

SPSSCompare H1, H2, and H3 with the workbook Parts A, B, C

Run the supplied .sps file and open its Viewer output. Match H1 to Part A, H2 to Part B, and H3 to Part C. For H2 and H3, read the uncorrected Pearson row when reconciling a two-proportion test.

PythonRecompute the in-class tests and net impact Parts A, B, C

Run this in the folder with the supplied CSV files. It finds the survey and checkout columns, prints in-class calculations only, and makes no launch choice. It expects one row per eligible checkout user and one score per recorded survey response.

import glob, math, re
import pandas as pd

files = [pd.read_csv(path) for path in sorted(glob.glob('*.csv'))]
if not files:
    raise FileNotFoundError('Run this in the folder with the supplied CSV files.')
def key(s): return re.sub('[^a-z0-9]', '', str(s).lower())
def column(df, names):
    for c in df.columns:
        if key(c) in names: return c
    return None
score_names = {'satisfaction', 'satisfactionscore', 'satisfactionpoints', 'satscore'}
group_names = {'group', 'arm', 'variant', 'experimentgroup'}
buy_names = {'purchase', 'purchased', 'converted', 'conversion', 'orderplaced'}
complaint_names = {'complaint', 'complained', 'hascomplaint', 'complaintflag'}
surveys = [(d, column(d, score_names)) for d in files if column(d, score_names)]
checkouts = [(d, column(d, group_names), column(d, buy_names), column(d, complaint_names)) for d in files if column(d, group_names) and column(d, buy_names) and column(d, complaint_names)]
if not surveys or not checkouts:
    raise ValueError('Check the supplied CSV headers for satisfaction, group, purchase, and complaint columns.')
survey, sc = surveys[0]
checkout, gc, bc, cc = checkouts[0]
scores = pd.to_numeric(survey[sc], errors='coerce').dropna()
n = len(scores); mean = scores.mean(); sd = scores.std(ddof=1)
if n < 2: raise ValueError('At least two recorded satisfaction scores are needed.')
t = (mean - 70) / (sd / math.sqrt(n))
df = n - 1
const = math.exp(math.lgamma((df+1)/2)-math.lgamma(df/2)) / math.sqrt(df*math.pi)
def density(v): return const * (1 + v*v/df)**(-(df+1)/2)
steps = 10000; h = abs(t)/steps
area = h/3 * (density(0) + density(abs(t)) + 4*sum(density(j*h) for j in range(1, steps, 2)) + 2*sum(density(j*h) for j in range(2, steps, 2)))
p_t = max(0.0, 1 - 2*area)
print(f'Part A: n={n}, mean={mean:.3f}, SE={sd/math.sqrt(n):.3f}, t={t:.3f}, two-sided p={p_t:.4f}')
arm = checkout[gc].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper()
if not arm.isin(['A', 'B']).all(): raise ValueError('Checkout groups must be A or B.')
def yes(series):
    v = series.astype(str).str.strip().str.lower()
    if not v.isin(['1','0','yes','no','y','n','true','false']).all():
        raise ValueError('Purchase and complaint flags must be recorded for each eligible user.')
    return v.isin(['1','yes','y','true'])
buy = yes(checkout[bc]); complaint = yes(checkout[cc])
na = (arm == 'A').sum(); nb = (arm == 'B').sum()
xa = int(buy[arm == 'A'].sum()); xb = int(buy[arm == 'B'].sum())
ca = int(complaint[arm == 'A'].sum()); cb = int(complaint[arm == 'B'].sum())
pa, pb = xa/na, xb/nb
pooled = (xa+xb)/(na+nb)
se0 = math.sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)*(1/na+1/nb))
z = (pb-pa)/se0
p_z = math.erfc(abs(z)/math.sqrt(2))
se_effect = math.sqrt(pa*(1-pa)/na + pb*(1-pb)/nb)
print(f'Part B: A {xa}/{na}, B {xb}/{nb}; pooled={pooled:.4f}; z={z:.3f}; p={p_z:.4f}')
print(f'Part B: B-minus-A gap={pb-pa:.4f}; 95% interval=({pb-pa-1.96*se_effect:.4f}, {pb-pa+1.96*se_effect:.4f}); Pearson={z*z:.3f}')
ra, rb = ca/na, cb/nb
net = (xb-xa)*12 - nb*0.60 - (cb-ca)*25
print(f'Part C: complaints A {ca}/{na}, B {cb}/{nb}; gap={rb-ra:.4f}; net=${net:.2f}')
RRecompute the in-class tests and net impact Parts A, B, C

This base R script reads the supplied CSV files in the current folder. It prints the in-class quantities only. It does not fill a dropdown or decide whether to launch.

paths <- list.files(pattern = '\\.csv$', ignore.case = TRUE)
if (!length(paths)) stop('Run this in the folder with the supplied CSV files.')
files <- lapply(paths, function(p) read.csv(p, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
key <- function(x) gsub('[^a-z0-9]', '', tolower(x))
col <- function(d, names) { hit <- which(key(names(d)) %in% names); if (length(hit)) hit[1] else NA_integer_ }
sn <- c('satisfaction','satisfactionscore','satisfactionpoints','satscore')
gn <- c('group','arm','variant','experimentgroup')
bn <- c('purchase','purchased','converted','conversion','orderplaced')
cn <- c('complaint','complained','hascomplaint','complaintflag')
si <- which(vapply(files, function(d) !is.na(col(d,sn)), logical(1)))[1]
ci <- which(vapply(files, function(d) all(!is.na(c(col(d,gn),col(d,bn),col(d,cn)))), logical(1)))[1]
if (is.na(si) || is.na(ci)) stop('Check CSV headers for satisfaction, group, purchase, and complaint.')
survey <- files[[si]]; checkout <- files[[ci]]
scores <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(survey[[col(survey,sn)]]))
scores <- scores[!is.na(scores)]; n <- length(scores)
if (n < 2) stop('At least two recorded scores are needed.')
se <- sd(scores)/sqrt(n); t <- (mean(scores)-70)/se
cat(sprintf('Part A: n=%d, mean=%.3f, SE=%.3f, t=%.3f, two-sided p=%.4f\n', n, mean(scores), se, t, 2*pt(-abs(t), n-1)))
arm <- toupper(trimws(as.character(checkout[[col(checkout,gn)]])))
if (!all(arm %in% c('A','B'))) stop('Checkout groups must be A or B.')
yes <- function(v) {
  v <- tolower(trimws(as.character(v)))
  if (!all(v %in% c('1','0','yes','no','y','n','true','false'))) stop('Purchase and complaint flags must be recorded.')
  v %in% c('1','yes','y','true')
}
buy <- yes(checkout[[col(checkout,bn)]]); complaint <- yes(checkout[[col(checkout,cn)]])
na <- sum(arm=='A'); nb <- sum(arm=='B')
xa <- sum(buy[arm=='A']); xb <- sum(buy[arm=='B'])
ca <- sum(complaint[arm=='A']); cb <- sum(complaint[arm=='B'])
pa <- xa/na; pb <- xb/nb; pooled <- (xa+xb)/(na+nb)
se0 <- sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)*(1/na+1/nb)); z <- (pb-pa)/se0
se.effect <- sqrt(pa*(1-pa)/na + pb*(1-pb)/nb)
cat(sprintf('Part B: A %d/%d, B %d/%d; pooled=%.4f; z=%.3f; p=%.4f\n', xa,na,xb,nb,pooled,z,2*pnorm(-abs(z))))
cat(sprintf('Part B: gap=%.4f; 95%% interval=(%.4f, %.4f); Pearson=%.3f\n', pb-pa,pb-pa-1.96*se.effect,pb-pa+1.96*se.effect,z^2))
net <- (xb-xa)*12 - nb*0.60 - (cb-ca)*25
cat(sprintf('Part C: complaints A %d/%d, B %d/%d; gap=%.4f; net=$%.2f\n', ca,na,cb,nb,cb/nb-ca/na,net))

Topic 2 · How precise is the satisfaction mean? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

ExcelAdd an interval for the recorded survey mean Parts A

In a copy of Part A, calculate a 95% interval in spare cells with =B8-T.INV.2T(0.05,B12)*B9 and =B8+T.INV.2T(0.05,B12)*B9. Compare its bounds with the goal in D7. Explain why this interval still does not make the respondents representative.

SPSSRead the H1 mean interval Parts A

In the supplied .sps output, revisit H1’s one-sample tables. Locate the confidence interval for the mean difference from the goal. Add the goal back to each bound if you want bounds for the mean itself.

PythonBootstrap the recorded mean Parts A

Resample the recorded survey scores to see how the sample mean moves. This is a precision exercise, not a cure for an unrepresentative survey.

import glob, re
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def key(x): return re.sub('[^a-z0-9]', '', str(x).lower())
names = {'satisfaction','satisfactionscore','satisfactionpoints','satscore'}
scores = None
for path in sorted(glob.glob('*.csv')):
    d = pd.read_csv(path)
    for c in d.columns:
        if key(c) in names:
            scores = pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors='coerce').dropna().to_numpy()
            break
    if scores is not None: break
if scores is None or len(scores) < 2: raise ValueError('Find the supplied CSV with recorded satisfaction scores.')
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
means = np.array([rng.choice(scores, size=len(scores), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)])
print('Recorded mean:', scores.mean(), '95% bootstrap interval:', np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5]))
print('This interval does not establish that respondents represent all users.')
RBootstrap the recorded mean Parts A

Use base R to resample the survey scores. Keep sampling precision separate from survey coverage.

key <- function(x) gsub('[^a-z0-9]', '', tolower(x))
namesWanted <- c('satisfaction','satisfactionscore','satisfactionpoints','satscore')
scores <- NULL
for (path in list.files(pattern='\\.csv$', ignore.case=TRUE)) {
  d <- read.csv(path, check.names=FALSE)
  hit <- which(key(names(d)) %in% namesWanted)
  if (length(hit)) { scores <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d[[hit[1]]])); scores <- scores[!is.na(scores)]; break }
}
if (is.null(scores) || length(scores)<2) stop('Find the supplied CSV with recorded satisfaction scores.')
set.seed(2026)
means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(scores, size=length(scores), replace=TRUE)))
print(c(recorded.mean=mean(scores), quantile(means,c(.025,.975))))
cat('This interval does not establish that respondents represent all users.\n')

Topic 3 · Are purchases and complaints associated within each arm? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

ExcelMake two purchase-by-complaint tables Parts B, C

In a copy, make a PivotTable from Checkout. Filter to A and place purchase and complaint flags on rows and columns; repeat for B. Show counts, not just percentages. For each two-by-two table, compare observed counts with counts expected from its row and column totals before using CHISQ.TEST.

SPSSSeparate the two arm tables Parts B, C

After running the supplied .sps, use the checkout data it opens. Split output by group, then run CROSSTABS with purchase by complaint, observed and expected counts, and Pearson chi-square. Turn Split File off afterward. An association within an arm does not establish its cause.

PythonInspect within-arm two-by-two tables Parts B, C

This looks for a purchase–complaint association separately in A and B. It is not another estimate of the checkout treatment effect.

import glob, math, re
import pandas as pd

def key(x): return re.sub('[^a-z0-9]', '', str(x).lower())
def find(d, options): return next((c for c in d.columns if key(c) in options), None)
group = {'group','arm','variant','experimentgroup'}
buy = {'purchase','purchased','converted','conversion','orderplaced'}
complaint = {'complaint','complained','hascomplaint','complaintflag'}
found = None
for path in sorted(glob.glob('*.csv')):
    d = pd.read_csv(path)
    cols = [find(d, group),find(d, buy),find(d, complaint)]
    if all(cols): found = (d, cols); break
if found is None: raise ValueError('Find group, purchase, and complaint columns in the supplied CSV files.')
d, (gc,bc,cc) = found
for arm in ('A','B'):
    part = d[d[gc].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper().eq(arm)]
    table = pd.crosstab(part[bc].astype(str).str.lower(), part[cc].astype(str).str.lower())
    print('\nArm',arm,'\n',table)
    if table.shape != (2,2):
        print('A two-by-two Pearson test needs both observed flag values.'); continue
    obs = table.to_numpy(); expected = obs.sum(axis=1)[:,None]*obs.sum(axis=0)[None,:]/obs.sum()
    if (expected == 0).any():
        print('An expected cell is zero; do not calculate Pearson chi-square.'); continue
    chi2 = ((obs-expected)**2/expected).sum()
    print('Pearson chi-square:',chi2,'p:',math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi2/2)))
print('Association within an arm does not establish cause.')
RInspect within-arm two-by-two tables Parts B, C

Use a separate purchase-by-complaint table for each arm. Treat small expected counts as a reason to question the Pearson approximation.

key <- function(x) gsub('[^a-z0-9]', '', tolower(x))
find <- function(d, choices) { hit <- which(key(names(d)) %in% choices); if(length(hit)) hit[1] else NA_integer_ }
gn <- c('group','arm','variant','experimentgroup')
bn <- c('purchase','purchased','converted','conversion','orderplaced')
cn <- c('complaint','complained','hascomplaint','complaintflag')
d <- NULL
for (path in list.files(pattern='\\.csv$', ignore.case=TRUE)) {
  candidate <- read.csv(path, check.names=FALSE, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  if(all(!is.na(c(find(candidate,gn),find(candidate,bn),find(candidate,cn))))) { d <- candidate; break }
}
if(is.null(d)) stop('Find group, purchase, and complaint columns in the supplied CSV files.')
arm <- toupper(trimws(as.character(d[[find(d,gn)]])))
for (a in c('A','B')) {
  rows <- arm==a
  tab <- table(Purchase=d[[find(d,bn)]][rows], Complaint=d[[find(d,cn)]][rows])
  cat('\nArm',a,'\n'); print(tab)
  if(all(dim(tab)==c(2,2)) && all(rowSums(tab)>0) && all(colSums(tab)>0)) {
    test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct=FALSE))
    print(test$expected); print(test)
  } else cat('A two-by-two Pearson test needs both observed flag values.\n')
}
cat('Association within an arm does not establish cause.\n')

Topic 4 · Was the intended assignment balance preserved? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

ExcelAudit a planned equal split Parts B

If the assignment plan specified equal arms, use Part B B7:B8 to find the expected count per arm: (B7+B8)/2. In a copy, calculate the sum of each arm’s squared observed-minus-expected gap divided by that expected count. Apply CHISQ.DIST.RT with one degree of freedom. This checks allocation balance, not purchase performance.

SPSSCheck counts against the assignment plan Parts B

Use the checkout dataset opened by the supplied .sps. First inspect group frequencies for missing or duplicate user records. If the documented plan was an equal split, compare the observed A and B counts with that plan using a one-sample chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Do not infer the plan from the observed counts.

PythonCheck a documented equal-allocation plan Parts B

Use this only if the assignment plan called for equal A and B arms. This balance audit says nothing by itself about the purchase effect.

import glob, math, re
import pandas as pd

def key(x): return re.sub('[^a-z0-9]', '', str(x).lower())
d = None; gc = None
for path in sorted(glob.glob('*.csv')):
    candidate = pd.read_csv(path)
    names = {key(c):c for c in candidate.columns}
    hit = next((names[x] for x in ('group','arm','variant','experimentgroup') if x in names), None)
    if hit is not None: d, gc = candidate, hit; break
if d is None: raise ValueError('Find the supplied checkout CSV with a group column.')
arm = d[gc].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper()
if not arm.isin(['A','B']).all(): raise ValueError('Inspect missing or unexpected assignment labels first.')
a, b = int(arm.eq('A').sum()), int(arm.eq('B').sum())
expected = (a+b)/2
chi2 = (a-expected)**2/expected + (b-expected)**2/expected
print('Eligible assignment counts:',a,b)
print('Equal-split chi-square:',chi2,'p:',math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi2/2)))
print('Use this check only if equal allocation was the documented plan.')
RCheck a documented equal-allocation plan Parts B

Compare eligible-user arm counts with an equal split only if that was the assignment plan. This is an assignment audit, not an outcome test.

key <- function(x) gsub('[^a-z0-9]', '', tolower(x))
d <- NULL; gc <- NULL
for(path in list.files(pattern='\\.csv$', ignore.case=TRUE)) {
  candidate <- read.csv(path, check.names=FALSE, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  hit <- which(key(names(candidate)) %in% c('group','arm','variant','experimentgroup'))
  if(length(hit)) { d <- candidate; gc <- hit[1]; break }
}
if(is.null(d)) stop('Find the supplied checkout CSV with a group column.')
arm <- toupper(trimws(as.character(d[[gc]])))
if(!all(arm %in% c('A','B'))) stop('Inspect missing or unexpected assignment labels first.')
counts <- table(factor(arm, levels=c('A','B')))
print(counts)
print(chisq.test(counts, p=c(.5,.5)))
cat('Use this check only if equal allocation was the documented plan.\n')
